name: Maya, Chan Santa Cruz
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired Glottolog languoid, merged into Yucatec [yua] 2009; only ISO change-request document exists

new_statements.quote: Accent in Modern Yucatec appears to be determined lexically; with few exceptions, a sharp division can be made between those verbs in which the stem is accented, regardless of whether one, two, or more suffixes are added, and those whose stem is invariably unaccented. Regarding nouns, somewhat more complex behavior is noted. [...] Words with one double vowel; the accent is always on the first element. [...] (a) The most frequent pattern for disyllabic noun and verb forms is that in which the ultima bears the accent. [...] (b) The accent falls on the penult in a small number of nouns and verbs; and in all words which contain a double vowel in the penult.
new_statements.citation: Andrade, Manuel J. 1955. A Grammar of Modern Yucatec. Microfilm Collection of Manuscripts on Middle American Cultural Anthropology, No. 41. Chicago: University of Chicago Library (ms. completed before 1941; online edition ed. Christian Lehmann,https://www.christianlehmann.eu/ling/sprachen/maya/andrade/andrade_edit.php). Part 1, sec. 1.6 'Accent'.
new_statements.locator: Part 1, sec. 1.6 'Accent' (Lehmann's online edition has no page numbers; lines 848-1095). Quintana Roo informants (Chunpon, Bacalar, Icayche): introduction sec. 4 'Speech differences' and the text-list paragraph, the text.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Andrade treats accent as a lexical property of stems (accented vs. unaccented verb stems; nouns more complex), with strong tendencies: a double-vowel (long) syllable always carries the accent; otherwise disyllables are mostly final-accented (ʧaˈmal 'cigarette', binlaˈhoːb 'they all went'), a smaller lexical set penult-accented (ˈulum 'turkey', ˈmakan 'grove'); trisyllables are either final-accented or antepenult-primary + final-secondary; words of four or more syllables are always final-accented with a secondary accent on the first or second syllable. So: lexically assigned, with long vowels attracting it and final as the default; Kidder 2013 (sec. 3.3.2) reinterprets Andrade's penult 'accent' as the high tone of long vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Marked explicitly (ˌ): 'Primary and secondary accents are observed on penult and ultima, respectively, of compound nouns and of nouns which are followed by -a', -e', -o', or -ben'; trisyllable pattern (b) = primary on the antepenult, secondary on the ultima; in words of more than three syllables 'the ultima is invariably accented; in most instances either the first or second syllable is also accented' (e.g. ˈk'ek'enoːˌboʔ 'pigs').
new_statements.exceptions: 'with few exceptions'; a list of 'accentual irregularities observed in the texts' (ku ts'aabal, in hante, kimen, hok'en, hanen, lubaan, ch'aben, ma chuukul); trisyllables fitting neither pattern (k'alaanen, k'axlantaal, sukune', binechi, okk'iine', koleltsil). Andrade also warns that pitch vs. accent 'has not been studied sufficiently' and that greater stress often accompanies lower pitch.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level 'relative stress within a word', observed in recorded texts (connected speech from 32 informants across Yucatán, Campeche, Belize and Quintana Roo), not elicited citation forms; not specific to the Chan Santa Cruz area, though Quintana Roo speakers (Chunpon, Bacalar, Icayche) are among the informants and their speech is the conservative 'Type A' on which the grammar is based. Pre-1941 auditory description; modern instrumental work on the same language (Kidder 2013, Western dialect) finds no obligatory word stress and treats the long-vowel H/L contrast as tone.
new_statements.identity_note: maya1286 is not a distinct language. It is the Glottolog bookkeeping record for ISO 639-3 [yus] 'Chan Santa Cruz Maya', an Ethnologue dialect name for the Maya of the Chan Santa Cruz / Cruzo'ob region of central Quintana Roo (Felipe Carrillo Puerto, Yaxley, Chunpon, Señor, Tihosuco), retired by change request 2008-063 (N. England) and merged into [yua] Yucatec Maya = Glottolog yuca1254 on 2009-01-16. Glottolog attaches no descriptive reference to it. Yucatec Maya (yuca1254) is already in the catalog (deciding source Kidder 2013, classification tonal-OR-pitch accent). The variety [yus] denoted corresponds to Lehmann's 'variedad de la zona maya' (Yaxley data of Kügler, Skopeteas & Verhoeven 2006/2007; Bohnemeyer; Verhoeven) and to Frazier's 'Eastern dialect', which Kidder 2013 (after Frazier 2009) reports as lacking the consistent H/L tone contrast of the Western (Mérida/Santa Elena/Oxkutzcab) dialect on which Kidder's no-word-stress result rests.

new_statements.quote: Stress is noncontrastive in Yucatec Maya. However, there are no comprehensive studies of stress, and there are some disagreements in the literature about exactly where stress occurs. B et al. say "In words of more than one syllable, the syllable containing a long vowel is stressed. If the word has two long vowels, the vowel in the first syllable receives primary stress. If the word has no long vowel, the last syllable is stressed." (Bricker et al. 1998: xiii) [...] Generalizing from the above statements, we can conclude that heavy syllables and the leftmost syllable attract stress in Yucatec Maya.
new_statements.citation: Frazier, Melissa. 2009. The production and perception of pitch and glottalization in Yucatec Maya. PhD dissertation, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

new_statements.relation_note: maya1286 has no catalog record; the one existing statement is Andrade 1955 ('Accent in Modern Yucatec appears to be determined lexically', read as lexical (unpredictable)). Frazier types stress as NONCONTRASTIVE and weight-driven (long vowels / leftmost; else final per Bricker), so the TYPE differs from Andrade's 'lexical' label, although the substance overlaps (Andrade too has double vowels attracting accent and otherwise mostly final accent). It agrees with the parent-language catalog entry yuca1254 (Kidder 2013: tone language, word stress disputed; Bricker default = leftmost long vowel else final). Frazier's statement is a literature summary for Yucatec Maya as a whole; her fieldwork sit…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not contrastive. Summarising the literature (Bricker et al. 1998, Blair & Vermont-Salas, Blair 1964), Frazier concludes that heavy syllables (long vowels; the always-closed final syllable also counts as bimoraic) and the leftmost syllable attract stress: a long-vowel syllable is stressed, with two long vowels the first is stressed, with none the final syllable (Bricker et al.); she notes the sources disagree on all-short disyllables (equal prominence per B&VS and Blair) and that clash resolution is undescribed. No stress experiment of her own; the dissertation is about pitch, length and glottalization (tone).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only via Blair 1964 as reported: in strings of short open syllables the first and every other syllable thereafter are stressed (alternating), except two-syllable strings where both are equally prominent; fn. 12: per Hanks 1984, unstressed or secondarily stressed syllables of Spanish loans receive high tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables of two short syllables: both syllables equal in intensity/prominence (Blair & Vermont-Salas; Blair 1964) rather than final stress (Bricker et al.). Dialect result relevant to type: eastern-Yucatán speakers (Sisbicchén, Xocén, Yax Che) show a likely HIGH/LOW tonal merger with HIGH TONE vowels longest (sec. 7.1.2), i.e. tone may be a dialectal feature; nothing is said about stress differing by dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: maya1286 'Maya, Chan Santa Cruz' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for retired ISO [yus], merged into Yucatec Maya [yua] (yuca1254) by ISO CR 2008-063 (2009); it denotes the Quintana Roo (Cruzo'ob / Felipe Carrillo Puerto) variety. Frazier 2009 describes Yucatec Maya as a language; her stress section is literature-based (Bricker et al. 1998 describe Hocabá Yucatec) and her own fieldwork was entirely in Yucatán state (western dialect: Mérida, Santa Elena; eastern dialect: Sisbicchén, Xocén, Yax Che near Valladolid), not Quintana Roo. Any catalog use should defer to the yuca1254 entry.

readall_conflicts: The sources for this (bookkeeping) Yucatec variety do not agree on the TYPE of word prominence. Andrade 1955 (grammar with Quintana Roo informants among 32) calls accent 'determined lexically' while giving tendencies (double vowel attracts accent; disyllables mostly final; words of more than three syllables final). Frazier 2009 sec. 1.2.6 (pp. 22-23), now opened, says 'Stress is noncontrastive in Yucatec Maya', summarises Bricker et al. 1998 (long-vowel syllable stressed, first of two long vowels, else final syllable), Blair & Vermont-Salas and Blair 1964 (all-short disyllables equally prominent; alternating stress in strings of short syllables), generalises that 'heavy syllables and the leftmost syllable attract stress', and states outright that the literature disagrees about where stress occurs and that no comprehensive study exists. Kidder 2013 (the yuca1254 catalog's deciding source; fn. 22: 'Stress in YM is not analyzed in Frazier (2009)', confirmed) finds no obligatory word-level stress at all. All treat Yucatec as having lexical tone on long vowels; Frazier adds that eastern-Yucatán speakers may have merged the H/L tone contrast into a length difference. The placement substance shared by Andrade, Bricker and Frazier is 'long vowel attracts prominence, otherwise final', but the labels (lexical vs noncontrastive weight-driven vs no word stress) conflict, so no single fixed reading is supported for maya1286 beyond what yuca1254 already records.

sources.note: Sec. 1.6 'Accent': accent 'appears to be determined lexically'; a double-vowel (long) syllable is always accented; disyllables mostly ultima (ʧaˈmal), penult in a lexical minority (ˈulum) and always when the penult has a double vowel; trisyllables ultima or antepenult+secondary ultima; 4+ syllables always ultima with a secondary on the 1st/2nd syllable (ˈk'ek'enoːˌboʔ). Informants include speakers from Chunpon, Bacalar and Icayche, Quintana Roo, whose speech is 'prevalently of Type A' (intro sec. 4).

sources.note: 'Yucatec Maya is a tone language, displaying a three-fold opposition in the tonal realization of syllables' (p. 187); long vowels are obligatory TBUs with H vs L, short vowels toneless (sec. 3.1, p. 191); 'Yucatec Maya does not employ additional pitch accents to express topic or focus' (sec. 3.4, p. 195).
